title: "The analysis"

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
voters <- wss |> filter(!is.na(trump_vote))
c(n_obs = nrow(voters), n_miss = nrow(wss) - nrow(voters), n_total = nrow(wss))
#>   n_obs  n_miss n_total 
#>    6495    1105    7600
```
:::


Every number below rests on those 6,495 respondents. Report that pair with every model
you show anyone, including yourself.

## Weighted two-party Trump share


::: {#tbl-shares .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Weighted two-party Trump share, by year and ethnicity.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
shares <- voters |>
  summarise(trump = weighted.mean(trump_vote, weight),
            n     = n(),
            n_eff = sum(weight)^2 / sum(weight^2),
            .by   = c(year, latino)) |>
  mutate(se        = sqrt(trump * (1 - trump) / n_eff),
         trump_low = trump - 1.96 * se,
         trump_upp = trump + 1.96 * se)

shares |>
  select(year, latino, trump, n, n_eff, trump_low, trump_upp) |>
  arrange(latino, year) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|year |latino     | trump|    n|    n_eff| trump_low| trump_upp|
|:----|:----------|-----:|----:|--------:|---------:|---------:|
|2020 |Non-Latino | 0.503| 1944| 1664.053|     0.478|     0.527|
|2024 |Non-Latino | 0.511| 2828| 2040.561|     0.490|     0.533|
|2020 |Latino     | 0.398|  937|  478.528|     0.354|     0.442|
|2024 |Latino     | 0.419|  786|  452.405|     0.374|     0.465|


:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(shares, aes(year, trump, colour = latino, group = latino)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = trump_low, ymax = trump_upp)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Two-party Trump share (weighted)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Two-party Trump share with 95% intervals from a Kish effective *n*.](08-analysis_files/figure-html/fig-shares-1.png){#fig-shares fig-align='center' width=900}
:::
:::


::: {.warn}
[The interval is approximate, and the approximation matters]{.warn-head}
`n_eff` is Kish's effective sample size, which discounts for unequal weights but ignores
clustering and stratification. For anything you would publish, use a design-based
variance:

```r
library(survey)
des <- svydesign(ids = ~1, weights = ~weight, data = voters)
svyby(~trump_vote, ~interaction(year, latino), des, svymean)
```

An agent asked for "confidence intervals on a weighted mean" will usually hand you the
Kish version without mentioning the assumption. That is not a bug in the agent; it is
the thing you are responsible for noticing.
:::

The Latino shift is about two points, on 786 Latino respondents in 2024 — nothing like
the double-digit national exit-poll story. Whether that is a real difference, a
weighting artifact, a mode difference, or the reported-versus-intended mix is the
interesting question, and this table cannot settle it alone.

## Does authoritarianism condition the shift?


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit <- glm(trump_vote ~ latino * year * authoritarianism + age + female + college,
           family = quasibinomial, weights = weight, data = voters)

c(n_obs = nobs(fit), n_miss = nrow(voters) - nobs(fit))
#>  n_obs n_miss 
#>   6494      1
```
:::


The model drops cases the descriptive table kept — listwise deletion on the covariates.
That gap is the single most common way a sample quietly shrinks.


::: {#tbl-coefs .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Quasibinomial logit coefficients.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
broom::tidy(fit) |>
  mutate(term = str_replace_all(term, c("latino" = "", "year" = "year "))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}

|:---------------------------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:|
|(Intercept)                       |   -1.020|     0.106|    -9.587|   0.000|
|Latino                            |   -0.063|     0.183|    -0.345|   0.730|
|year 2024                         |    0.113|     0.094|     1.192|   0.233|
|authoritarianism                  |    2.127|     0.142|    15.001|   0.000|
|age                               |    0.008|     0.001|     5.691|   0.000|
|female                            |   -0.360|     0.053|    -6.781|   0.000|

|Latino:year 2024:authoritarianism |    0.096|     0.403|     0.238|   0.812|


:::
:::


Interactions on the logit scale are close to unreadable, so look at predictions instead:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
grid <- expand_grid(
  latino           = levels(voters$latino),
  year             = levels(voters$year),
  authoritarianism = seq(0, 1, 0.05),
  age              = mean(voters$age, na.rm = TRUE),
  female           = 0,
  college          = 0
) |>
  mutate(latino = factor(latino, levels(voters$latino)),
         year   = factor(year, levels(voters$year)))

pred <- bind_cols(grid, as_tibble(predict(fit, grid, type = "link", se.fit = TRUE))) |>
  mutate(p   = plogis(fit),
         low = plogis(fit - 1.96 * se.fit),
         upp = plogis(fit + 1.96 * se.fit))

ggplot(pred, aes(authoritarianism, p, colour = year, fill = year)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = low, ymax = upp), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ latino) +
  labs(x = "Authoritarianism (0–1)", y = "Pr(Trump vote)",
       colour = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Predicted probability of a Trump vote across the authoritarianism scale.](08-analysis_files/figure-html/fig-pred-1.png){#fig-pred fig-align='center' width=1050}
:::
:::


Read it carefully: the question is not whether the lines slope — they do, in both groups
— but whether the *gap between years* changes across the scale. On this sample those
intervals are wide enough that honest answers include "we cannot tell."

## The Bayesian version

`brms` is the better tool here: priors on an interaction-heavy model, and posterior
summaries you can actually interpret. It is not run in the book because compiling takes
longer than the whole render.

```r
library(brms)
fit_b <- brm(
  trump_vote | weights(weight) ~ latino * year * authoritarianism +
    age + female + college,
  family  = bernoulli(),
  prior   = c(prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b"),
              prior(normal(0, 2), class = "Intercept")),
  data = voters, chains = 4, cores = 4, backend = "cmdstanr", seed = 1
)
fit_b                                            # n_obs is in the output header
pp_check(fit_b)
conditional_effects(fit_b, "authoritarianism:latino")
```

::: {.note}
[`weights()` in `brms` is not survey weighting]{.note-head}
It treats each weight as a case replication, which gives you the point estimates but
understates uncertainty for a complex design. If the weights carry a design, say so in
the paper, or move to a design-based estimator. This is worth stating out loud because
it is precisely the distinction an agent will flatten.
:::

The figures this chapter draws are also written to `output/` by `R/02_analysis.R`, which
is git-ignored — the repository keeps the script, not the picture.
